nodes.name: Half-Laplacian operator (Levy-Khintchine formula)
nodes.statement: Let us set the one-dimensional half-Laplacian operator $L$ defined on functions $w\in L^\infty (\hbox{\bf R})\cap C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\hbox{\bf R})$ for some $0<\beta<1$ by the L\'evy-Khintchine formula $$Lw(x)=\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{\hbox{\bf R}}\frac{dz}{z^2}\left(w(x+z)-w(x)-zw'(x) 1_{\left\{|z|\le 1\right\}}\right).$$
nodes.statement_short: Defines the one-dimensional half-Laplacian $L$ by the Levy-Khintchine integral formula.

nodes.name: Peierls-Nabarro layer problem
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{l} L\phi -W'(\phi)=0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad \hbox{\bf R},\\ \displaystyle{\phi'>0 \quad \mbox{and}\quad \phi(-\infty)=0,\quad \phi(0)=\frac 1 2,\quad \phi(+\infty)=1.} \end{array}\right.
nodes.statement_short: Layer solution $\phi$: $L\phi=W'(\phi)$, increasing from 0 to 1 with $\phi(0)=1/2$.
nodes.label: eq::0

nodes.name: Peierls-Nabarro model
nodes.statement: Model \eqref{eq::0} is known as the Peierls-Nabarro model for dislocations in crystals where $W$ is called the stacking fault energy.

nodes.name: Evolution equation for the Peierls-Nabarro model
nodes.statement: v_t=Lv-W'(v) + \sigma^\varepsilon(t,x) \quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}
nodes.label: eq::901

nodes.name: Scaling of the exterior stress
nodes.statement: We assume that this exterior stress is given for $\varepsilon>0$ small, by $$\sigma^\varepsilon(t,x)=\varepsilon\sigma\left(\frac{t}{\varepsilon^2},\frac{x}{\varepsilon}\right)$$ where $\sigma$ is a given suitable function.

nodes.name: Rescaled solution $v^\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: Then we can consider the following rescaling $$v^\varepsilon(t,x)=v\left(\frac{t}{\varepsilon^2},\frac{x}{\varepsilon}\right).$$

nodes.name: Rescaled reaction-diffusion equation with half-Laplacian
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{l} \displaystyle{v^\varepsilon_t=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{Lv^\varepsilon-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}W'(v^\varepsilon) + \sigma(t,x)\right\} \quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}}\\ \\ v^\varepsilon(0,x)=v^\varepsilon_0(x) \quad \mbox{for}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}. \end{array}\right.
nodes.statement_short: Rescaled evolution problem $v^\varepsilon_t=\varepsilon^{-1}(Lv^\varepsilon-\varepsilon^{-1}W'(v^\varepsilon)+\sigma)$ with initial data.
nodes.label: eq::1

nodes.name: ODE system for particles (dislocations)
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{lcl} \displaystyle{\frac{dx_i}{dt}}= \gamma \left(-\sigma(t,x_i) + \frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{j\not= i} \frac{1}{x_i-x_j}\right),\quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty),\\ x_i(0)=x_i^0, \end{array}\right| \quad \mbox{for}\quad i=1,...,N
nodes.statement_short: Particles move with velocity $\gamma$ times exterior stress plus $1/(\pi(x_i-x_j))$ two-body interactions.
nodes.label: eq::2

nodes.name: Mobility constant gamma
nodes.statement: \gamma = \left(\int_{\hbox{\bf R}}(\phi')^2\right)^{-1}.
nodes.label: eq::2'

nodes.name: Assumption (A) i): periodic potential
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf i) Assumption on the potential}\\ $$\left\{\begin{array}{l} W\in C^{2,\beta}(\hbox{\bf R}) \quad \mbox{for some}\quad 0<\beta<1,\\ \\ W(v+1)=W(v) \quad \mbox{for any}\quad v\in\hbox{\bf R},\\ \\ W=0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad\hbox{\bf Z},\\ \\ W>0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad\hbox{\bf R}\backslash \hbox{\bf Z},\\ \\ W''(0)>0. \end{array}\right.$$
nodes.statement_short: $W$ is $C^{2,\beta}$, 1-periodic, vanishes exactly on the integers, with $W''(0)>0$.

nodes.name: Assumption (A) ii): exterior stress
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf ii) Assumption on the exterior stress} $$\left\{\begin{array}{l} \sigma \in BUC\left([0,+\infty )\times \hbox{\bf R}\right) \quad \mbox{and for some}\quad 0<\beta<1 \quad \mbox{and}\quad K>0, \quad \mbox{we have}\\ \\ |\sigma_x|_{L^\infty ([0,+\infty )\times \hbox{\bf R})}\le K, \quad |\sigma_t|_{L^\infty ([0,+\infty )\times \hbox{\bf R})}\le K,\\ \\ |\sigma_x(t,x+h)-\sigma_x(t,x)|\le K |h|^\beta \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x,h\in\hbox{\bf R},\quad t\in [0,+\infty ). \end{array}\right.$$ We recall that BUC is the space of bounded uniformly continuous functions.
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma$ is bounded uniformly continuous, Lipschitz in $t$ and $x$, with $\sigma_x$ Holder in $x$.

nodes.name: Assumption (A) iii): well-prepared initial condition
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf iii) Assumption on the initial condition} \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{array}{l} \mbox{For}\quad x_1^0< x_2^0< ...<x^0_N, \quad \mbox{we set}\\ \\ \displaystyle{v_0^\varepsilon(x)=\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\sigma(0,x) + \sum_{i=1}^N \phi\left(\frac{x-x_i^0}{\varepsilon}\right) \quad \mbox{with}\quad \alpha=W''(0)>0.} \end{array}\right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Initial data is a sum of $N$ rescaled layers at ordered points plus $\varepsilon\sigma(0,x)/\alpha$, $\alpha=W''(0)$.

nodes.name: Initial condition and alpha = W''(0)
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{l} \mbox{For}\quad x_1^0< x_2^0< ...<x^0_N, \quad \mbox{we set}\\ \\ \displaystyle{v_0^\varepsilon(x)=\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\sigma(0,x) + \sum_{i=1}^N \phi\left(\frac{x-x_i^0}{\varepsilon}\right) \quad \mbox{with}\quad \alpha=W''(0)>0.} \end{array}\right.
nodes.label: eq::900

nodes.name: Convergence to the ODE system
nodes.statement: {\bf (Convergence to the ODE system)}\\ Under assumption (A), there exists a unique solution $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ of (\ref{eq::2}). Let $$v^0(t,x)= \sum_{i=1}^N H(x-x_i(t))$$ where $H(x)=1_{[0,+\infty)}(x)$ is the Heaviside function. Then for any $\varepsilon >0$, there exists a unique viscosity solution $v^\varepsilon$ of (\ref{eq::1}). Moreover as $\varepsilon \to 0$, $v^\varepsilon$ converges to $v^0$ in the following sense: \begin{equation} \limsup_{(t',x')\to(t,x),\ \epsilon\to 0} v^{\epsilon}(t',x')\leq (v^0)^* (t,x) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \liminf_{(t',x')\to(t,x),\ \epsilon\to 0} v^{\epsilon}(t',x')\geq (v^0)_* (t,x) \end{equation} for $(t,x)\in [0,+\infty )\times \hbox{\bf R}$.
conclusions: there exists a unique solution $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ of (\ref{eq::2})
for any $\varepsilon >0$, there exists a unique viscosity solution $v^\varepsilon$ of (\ref{eq::1})
as $\varepsilon \to 0$, $v^\varepsilon$ converges to $v^0$ in the following sense: \begin{equation} \limsup_{(t',x')\to(t,x),\ \epsilon\to 0} v^{\epsilon}(t',x')\leq (v^0)^* (t,x) \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Under (A), $v^\varepsilon$ exists uniquely and converges (via semicontinuous envelopes) to a sum of Heavisides at the ODE particle positions.
nodes.label: th::1

nodes.name: Upper convergence bound
nodes.statement: \limsup_{(t',x')\to(t,x),\ \epsilon\to 0} v^{\epsilon}(t',x')\leq (v^0)^* (t,x)
nodes.label: eq::c+

nodes.name: Lower convergence bound
nodes.statement: \liminf_{(t',x')\to(t,x),\ \epsilon\to 0} v^{\epsilon}(t',x')\geq (v^0)_* (t,x)
nodes.label: eq::c-

nodes.name: Semi-continuous envelopes
nodes.statement: We recall here that the semi-continuous envelopes of a given any function $u$ are defined as follows $$u^*(t,x)=\limsup_{(t',x')\to(t,x)} u(t',x')\quad\quad\mbox{and}\quad\quad u_*(t,x)=\liminf_{(t',x')\to(t,x)} u(t',x').$$

nodes.name: Ansatz for the solution
nodes.statement: \tilde{v}^\varepsilon(t,x)=\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\sigma(t,x)+\sum_{i=1}^N \left\{ \phi\left(\frac{x-x_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right)-\varepsilon \dot{x}_i(t)\ \psi\left(\frac{x-x_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) \right\}
nodes.statement_short: Ansatz: $\varepsilon\sigma/\alpha$ plus layers at $x_i(t)$ minus $\varepsilon\dot x_i$ times the corrector $\psi$.
nodes.label: eq::an

nodes.name: Alberti-Bouchitte-Seppecher Gamma-convergence
nodes.statement: They have shown in \cite{Alberti-Bouchitte-Seppecher:singular-perturbations} that if we consider the energy functional for $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ and a double well potential $W$ given by $$E_\epsilon[u]=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u}^2+\frac{1}{\epsilon}\int_{\partial\Omega}W(u)$$ then, in particular, the rescalings $E_\epsilon[u]/\abs{\log\epsilon}$ Gamma-converge when $\epsilon\to 0$ to $\frac{2}{\pi}\mathcal H^0(S_{u_0})$ if $n=2$ (thus $\partial\Omega$ is one dimensional) and the minimizers $u_\epsilon$ converge to $u_0$, where $u_0=0,1$ on $\partial\Omega$, $\Delta u_0=0$ in $\Omega$, and the singular set is $$S_{u_0}=\left\{ z\in\partial\Omega \mbox{ : }u_0 \mbox{ jumps at }z \right\}.$$
assumptions: if we consider the energy functional for $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ and a double well potential $W$ given by $$E_\epsilon[u]=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u}^2+\frac{1}{\epsilon}\int_{\partial\Omega}W(u)$$
conclusions: the rescalings $E_\epsilon[u]/\abs{\log\epsilon}$ Gamma-converge when $\epsilon\to 0$ to $\frac{2}{\pi}\mathcal H^0(S_{u_0})$ if $n=2$

the minimizers $u_\epsilon$ converge to $u_0$, where $u_0=0,1$ on $\partial\Omega$, $\Delta u_0=0$ in $\Omega$, and the singular set is $$S_{u_0}=\left\{ z\in\partial\Omega \mbox{ : }u_0 \mbox{ jumps at }z \right\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: $E_\epsilon/|\log\epsilon|$ Gamma-converges to $\frac{2}{\pi}$ times the counting measure of the jump set of the boundary trace.

nodes.name: Extension to fractional Laplacians
nodes.statement: We expect (even if we have no proof) Theorem \ref{th::1} to be true for any power of the Laplacian $(-\Delta)^\alpha$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$, once the layer solutions of \eqref{eq::0} are found.
assumptions: for any power of the Laplacian $(-\Delta)^\alpha$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$
once the layer solutions of \eqref{eq::0} are found
conclusions: Theorem \ref{th::1} to be true
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1.1 should hold for $(-\Delta)^\alpha$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$, once layer solutions exist.

nodes.name: Evolution problem with epsilon = 1
nodes.statement: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \displaystyle{v_t=Lv-W'(v) + \sigma(t,x) \quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}}\\ v(0,x)=v_0(x) \quad \mbox{for}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}. \end{array}\right.
nodes.label: eq::1ter

nodes.name: Viscosity sub and supersolutions
nodes.statement: {\bf (Viscosity sub and supersolutions)}\\ An upper (respectively lower) semicontinuous function $v\in L^\infty([0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R})$ is said to be a subsolution (resp. a supersolution) of (\ref{eq::1ter}) if and only if $$v(0,\cdot)\le v_0^* \quad \mbox{on}\quad \hbox{\bf R}$$ $$\left(\mbox{resp.}\quad v(0,\cdot)\ge v_0^* \quad \mbox{on}\quad \hbox{\bf R}\right)$$ and for any $C^2$ test function $\varphi$ satisfying $$v= \varphi \quad \mbox{at the point}\quad (t_0,x_0)\in (0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}$$ and $$ v\le \varphi \quad \mbox{on a neighborhood of}\quad \left\{t_0\right\}\times \hbox{\bf R}$$ $$\left(\mbox{resp.}\quad v\ge \varphi \quad \mbox{on a neighborhood of}\quad \left\{t_0\right\}\times \hbox{\bf R}\right)$$ then we have $$\varphi_t(t_0,x_0) \le L^1[\varphi(t_0,\cdot),v(t_0,\cdot)](x_0) -W'(\varphi(t_0,x_0)) + \sigma(t_0,x_0)$$ $$\left(\mbox{resp.}\quad \varphi_t(t_0,x_0) \ge L^1[\varphi(t_0,\cdot),v(t_0,\cdot)](x_0) -W'(\varphi(t_0,x_0)) + \sigma(t_0,x_0) \right)$$ where for any functions $\Phi(x), w(x)$ we set $$L^1[\Phi,w](x_0)=\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{[-1,1]}\frac{dz}{z^2}\left(\Phi(x_0+z)-\Phi(x_0)-z\Phi'(x_0) \right) + \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{\hbox{\bf R}\backslash [-1,1]}\frac{dz}{z^2}\left(w(x_0+z)-w(x_0)\right).$$ A function $v\in L^\infty([0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R})$ is said to be a viscosity solution of (\ref{eq::1ter}), if and only if $v^*$ is a subsolution and $v_*$ is a supersolution.\\ Finally, a function $v\in L^\infty_{loc}([0,+\infty )\times \hbox{\bf R})$ is said to be a viscosity solution on $[0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}$, if and only if its is a viscosity solution on $[0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}$ for any $T>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Test-function definition of viscosity sub/supersolutions for the nonlocal equation, with $L$ split into a local part on $\varphi$ and a far part on $v$.
nodes.label: defi::1

nodes.name: Classical solutions are viscosity solutions
nodes.statement: {\bf (Classical solutions are viscosity solutions)}\\ From this definition, we can easily check that every function $v\in L^\infty([0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R})\cap C^{1,\beta}_{loc}([0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R})$ for some $0<\beta<1$, is indeed a viscosity solution if and only if it is a classical solution of (\ref{eq::1ter}). This is mainly due to the fact that $v_t$ and $Lv(t,\cdot)$ are then defined pointwise.

nodes.name: Perron's method
nodes.statement: {\bf (Perron's method)}\\ Assume that there exists a supersolution $\underline{v}$ and a subsolution $\overline{v}$ of equation (\ref{eq::1ter}) satisfying $$\underline{v} \le \overline{v} \quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}.$$ Then there exists a viscosity solution $v$ of (\ref{eq::1ter}) satisfying $$\underline{v} \le v\le \overline{v} \quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}.$$
assumptions: there exists a supersolution $\underline{v}$ and a subsolution $\overline{v}$ of equation (\ref{eq::1ter}) satisfying $$\underline{v} \le \overline{v} \quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}.$$
conclusions: there exists a viscosity solution $v$ of (\ref{eq::1ter}) satisfying $$\underline{v} \le v\le \overline{v} \quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}.$$

nodes.name: Comparison principle
nodes.statement: {\bf (Comparison principle)}\\ Assume that $\underline{v}$ is a subsolution (resp. $\overline{v}$ is a supersolution) of equation (\ref{eq::1ter}) on $[0,T)$ such that $$\underline{v}(0,x)\le \overline{v}(0,x)\quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in \hbox{\bf R}.$$ Then $$\underline{v}\le \overline{v}\quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}.$$

conclusions: $$\underline{v}\le \overline{v}\quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)

nodes.name: Uniqueness and continuity from comparison
nodes.statement: In particular, when the initial data $v_0$ is continuous, the comparison principle implies the uniqueness and the continuity of the solution.
assumptions: when the initial data $v_0$ is continuous
conclusions: the comparison principle implies the uniqueness and the continuity of the solution

nodes.name: Formal derivation of the ansatz
nodes.statement: In the following, we try to explain formally why we have to expect an ansatz as in \eqref{eq::an} for the solutions of \eqref{eq::1}. \medskip Namely, we are looking for an ansatz for the solutions of \begin{equation} \displaystyle{-\varepsilon v^\varepsilon_t=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{W'(v^\varepsilon) -\varepsilon Lv^\varepsilon - \varepsilon \sigma \right\}\quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}.} \end{equation} Assume to simplify that $\sigma$ is a constant here, and that there is only one transition layer.\\ \noindent {\bf First try for the ansatz}\\ As a first try, in the case where $\tilde{\sigma}$ is constant, we could consider the Ansatz $$\tilde{v}^\varepsilon(t,x)=\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \phi\left(\frac{x-x_1(t)}{\varepsilon}\right)$$ where $\phi$ is the transition layer solution of \begin{equation} L\phi-W'(\phi)=0. \end{equation} When we plug this expression in (\ref{eq::13}), we get $$\begin{array}{lcl} \dot{x}_1\phi' &\simeq &\displaystyle{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{W'(\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \phi) - L\phi -\varepsilon \sigma\right\}}\\ \\ & \simeq &\displaystyle{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{W'(\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \phi) - W'(\phi) -\varepsilon \sigma\right\}}\\ \\ & \simeq & \displaystyle{W''(\phi) \tilde{\sigma} -\sigma + O(\varepsilon)}\\ \end{array}$$ where we have used (\ref{eq::14}) for the second line, and a Taylor expansion to get the third line. From this computation, we learn two things. First for $\phi \simeq 0$ we have to choose \begin{equation} W''(0) \tilde{\sigma} =\sigma. \end{equation} The second information, is that it is impossible to satisfy the equation with this ansatz, and we need to introduce a corrector.\\ \noindent {\bf Second try for the ansatz}\\ Let us take $$\tilde{v}^\varepsilon(t,x)=\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \phi\left(\frac{x-x_1(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) -\varepsilon c \psi\left(\frac{x-x_1(t)}{\varepsilon}\right)$$ for $\tilde{\sigma}$ satisfying (\ref{eq::15}) and for some constant $c$ to fix later. When we plug this expression in (\ref{eq::13}), we get $$\begin{array}{lcl} \dot{x}_1\phi' +h.o.t. &\simeq &\displaystyle{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{W'(\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \phi -\varepsilon c\psi) - L\phi +c\varepsilon L\psi -\varepsilon \sigma\right\}}\\ \\ & \simeq &\displaystyle{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{W'(\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \phi -\varepsilon c\psi) - W'(\phi) +c\varepsilon L\psi -\varepsilon \sigma\right\}}\\ \\ & \simeq & W''(\phi) (\tilde{\sigma}-c\psi) -\sigma +c L\psi + h.o.t. \end{array}$$ where we have used a Taylor expansion to get the last line. Finally using (\ref{eq::15}), we see that $\psi$ has to solve \begin{equation} L\psi - W''(\phi)\psi = \frac{\dot{x}_1}{c} \phi' - \frac{\tilde{\sigma}}{c}(W''(\phi)-W''(0)). \end{equation} We see that it is convenient to choose (in order to get later $\psi$ independent on $\dot{x}_1$) $$\dot{x}_1=c.$$ Moreover, multiplying (\ref{eq::16}) by $\phi'$ we get formally by integration: $$\begin{array}{lcl} \displaystyle{\int_{\hbox{\bf R}} \phi'\left(L\psi - W''(\phi)\psi\right)} & = &\displaystyle{\int_{\hbox{\bf R}} (\phi')^2 -\frac{\tilde{\sigma}}{c} \left( \int_{\hbox{\bf R}} \frac{d}{dx}(W'(\phi(x)) - W''(0)\int_{\hbox{\bf R}} \phi'\right)}\\ \\ & = & \displaystyle{\int_{\hbox{\bf R}} (\phi')^2 +\frac{\tilde{\sigma}}{c} W''(0).} \end{array}$$ On the other hand using the fact that $L$ is self-adjoint, we get formally $$\begin{array}{lcl} \displaystyle{\int_{\hbox{\bf R}} \phi'\left(L\psi - W''(\phi)\psi\right)} &= &\displaystyle{\int_{\hbox{\bf R}} \psi\left(L\phi' - W''(\phi)\phi'\right)}\\ \\ &=& 0. \end{array}$$ where the last equality comes from the fact that $\phi$ solves (\ref{eq::14}) so then $\phi'$ solves $$L\phi'-W''(\phi)\phi'=0.$$ Therefore, we get $$c=-\gamma \sigma \quad \mbox{with}\quad \gamma= \left(\int_{\hbox{\bf R}}(\phi')^2\right)^{-1}$$ and $\psi$ solves $$L\psi - W''(\phi)\psi = \phi' +\eta (W''(\phi)-W''(0)) \quad \mbox{with}\quad \eta= \frac{1}{\gamma W''(0)}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Formal expansion: plugging the layer ansatz into the equation forces a corrector $\psi$ and the velocity $c=-\gamma\sigma$ via a solvability condition.

nodes.name: Lower bound on the distance between particles
nodes.statement: {\bf (Lower bound on the distance between particles, \cite{Forcadel-Imbert-Monneau:homogeneization})}\\ Let $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ be the solution of (\ref{eq::2bis}) on $[0,T]$ and let $$d(t):=\min\{\abs{x_i(t)-x_j(t)},i\neq j\}$$ be the minimal distance between particles. Then under assumptions Ai) and Aii), we have for all $t\in [0,T]$ $$d(t)\ge d(0) e^{-Ct} \quad \mbox{with}\quad C=\gamma K$$ where $K$ is the space Lipschitz constant of $\sigma$.
assumptions: Let $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ be the solution of (\ref{eq::2bis}) on $[0,T]$
conclusions: $$d(t)\ge d(0) e^{-Ct} \quad \mbox{with}\quad C=\gamma K$$
nodes.statement_short: The minimal interparticle distance decays at most exponentially: $d(t)\ge d(0)e^{-\gamma K t}$.

nodes.statement: {\bf (Long time existence of a solution to the ODE system)}\\ Under assumption (A), there exists a unique solution $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ of (\ref{eq::2bis}) on $[0,+\infty)$.
conclusions: there exists a unique solution $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ of (\ref{eq::2bis}) on $[0,+\infty)$

nodes.name: Perturbed particle trajectories $\overline{x}_i$
nodes.statement: We define $(\overline{x}_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ as the solution of $$\left\{\begin{array}{l} \displaystyle{\frac{d\overline{x}_i}{dt}= \gamma \left(-\delta-\sigma(\overline{x}_i,t) + \frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{j\not= i} \frac{1}{\overline{x}_i-\overline{x}_j}\right),\quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)},\\ \overline{x}_i(0)=x_i^0-\delta, \end{array}\right| \quad \mbox{for}\quad i=1,...,N$$ with $\gamma$ given in (\ref{eq::2'}).
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement_short: $\overline{x}_i$ solve the particle ODE with stress shifted by $\delta$ and initial positions shifted by $-\delta$.

nodes.name: Supersolution ansatz $\overline{v}^\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: We also define $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(t,x)=\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma}(t,x) + \sum_{i=1}^N \left\{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) -\varepsilon\overline{c}_i(t)\psi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) \right\}$$ where $$\left\{\begin{array}{l} \overline{c}_i(t) = \dot{\overline{x}}_i(t)\\ \\ \displaystyle{\tilde{\sigma}=\frac{\delta+\sigma}{\alpha} \quad \mbox{with}\quad \alpha=W''(0)>0} \end{array}\right.$$ and $\phi$ is given in Theorem \ref{th::5} and $\psi$ in Theorem \ref{th::6}.
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement_short: $\overline{v}^\varepsilon$ is the ansatz built on $\overline{x}_i$ with $\overline c_i=\dot{\overline x}_i$ and $\tilde\sigma=(\delta+\sigma)/\alpha$.

nodes.name: Supersolution at the initial time
nodes.statement: {\bf (Supersolution at the initial time)}\\ Under assumption (A), there exists $\delta_0>0$ such that for all $0<\delta\le \delta_0$, we have \begin{equation} \overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R} \end{equation} for $\varepsilon >0$ small enough.
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1
conclusions: there exists $\delta_0>0$ such that for all $0<\delta\le \delta_0$, we have \begin{equation} \overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R} \end{equation} for $\varepsilon >0$ small enough

nodes.name: Choose delta and A
nodes.statement: First we choose $\delta>0$ small enough such that $$x^0_i<\overline{x}_{i+1}(0)< x_{i+1}^0 \quad \mbox{for}\quad i=1,...,N-1.$$ Let $A>0$ be large enough such that \begin{equation} \frac{\delta}{\alpha} \ge \left(\sum_{i=1}^N |\overline{c}_i(0)|\right)\ \sup_{\hbox{\bf R}\backslash [-A,A]} |\psi|. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Fix $\delta$ so the shifted particles stay ordered and $A$ so $\psi$ is small outside $[-A,A]$.

nodes.name: Case 1: far from particles
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf Case 1: $|x-\overline{x}_i(0)|\ge \varepsilon A$ for each $i=1,...,N$}\\ Using the fact that $\phi$ is increasing, we deduce that $\displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_i(0)}{\varepsilon}\right) \ge \phi\left(\frac{x-{x}_i^0}{\varepsilon}\right)}$ and then using (\ref{eq::10}), we get that $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x).$$
nodes.statement_short: Far from all particles, monotonicity of $\phi$ and (eq 10) give the inequality.
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1

nodes.name: Case 2: near a particle
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf Case 2: $|x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)| < \varepsilon A$ for some index $i_0\in \left\{1,...,N\right\}$}\\ Then $$\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)}{\varepsilon}\right)\ge \phi(-A)>0$$ while $$\begin{array}{ll} \displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-{x}_{i_0}^0}{\varepsilon}\right)} & = \displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)-\delta}{\varepsilon}\right)}\\ \\ & \displaystyle{\le \phi\left(A-\frac{\delta}{\varepsilon}\right) = O\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right) \quad \mbox{as}\quad \varepsilon \to 0.} \end{array}$$ Therefore for $\varepsilon$ small enough, we have $$\displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)}{\varepsilon}\right) \ge \phi\left(\frac{x-{x}_{i_0}^0}{\varepsilon}\right) +\sum_{i=1}^N \varepsilon \overline{c}_i(0) \psi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i}(0)}{\varepsilon}\right)}.$$ Using again the monotonicity of $\phi$, we conclude in case 2 that $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x).$$
nodes.statement_short: Near a particle, $\phi(-A)>0$ dominates the $O(\varepsilon/\delta)$ term for small $\varepsilon$.
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Finally case 1 and 2 prove that (\ref{eq::8}) holds for any $x\in\hbox{\bf R}$. This ends the proof of the Proposition. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Both cases give (eq 8).

nodes.statement: We have, using the equation for the corrector, that $$\begin{array}{ll} I^\varepsilon = & \displaystyle{\left(\sum_{i=1}^N -\dot{\overline{x}}_i\phi'\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right)\right) + \left(\varepsilon\sum_{i=1}^N \left\{(\overline{c}_i)^2 \psi'\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) - \varepsilon\dot{\overline{c}}_i \psi_i\right\}\right) + \varepsilon^2 \tilde{\sigma}_t}\\ \\ & + \displaystyle{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}\left[\begin{array}{l} -\varepsilon^2 L \tilde{\sigma} -\varepsilon \sigma\\ \\ \displaystyle{+ W'\left(\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \sum_{i=1}^N \left\{\tilde{\phi}_i -\varepsilon \overline{c}_i \psi_i\right\}\right)}\\ \\ - \displaystyle{\sum_{i=1}^N \left\{W'(\tilde{\phi}_i) - \varepsilon \overline{c}_i \left[W''(\tilde{\phi}_i) \psi_i + \phi'\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) + \eta \left(W''(\tilde{\phi}_i)-W''(0)\right)\right]\right\}} \end{array}\right]. \end{array}$$
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the ansatz and the corrector equation into $I^\varepsilon$.
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1

nodes.name: Bound lower-order terms
nodes.statement: We first remark that all the terms in $\phi'$ vanish (because $\overline{c}_i=\dot{x}_i$). Using assumption (A), we can bound $\tilde{\sigma}_t, L\tilde{\sigma}$ and $\dot{\overline{c}}_i$. Moreover using Theorem \ref{th::6}, we can also bound $\psi'$. Finally, collecting all the terms of order $\varepsilon$ together, we get simply $$I^\varepsilon = O(\varepsilon) + \displaystyle{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}\left[\begin{array}{l} -\varepsilon \sigma\\ \\ \displaystyle{+ W'\left(\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \sum_{i=1}^N \left\{\tilde{\phi}_i -\varepsilon \overline{c}_i \psi_i\right\}\right)}\\ \\ - \displaystyle{\sum_{i=1}^N \left\{W'(\tilde{\phi}_i) - \varepsilon \overline{c}_i \left[W''(\tilde{\phi}_i) \psi_i + \eta \left(W''(\tilde{\phi}_i)-W''(0)\right)\right]\right\}.} \end{array}\right]$$
nodes.statement_short: Cancel $\phi'$ terms and bound remaining terms by $O(\varepsilon)$ using (A) and Theorem 3.2.

nodes.name: Collect terms
nodes.statement: We remark that the terms in $W'(\tilde{\phi}_{i_0})$ vanish and the terms in $\psi_{i_0}$ vanish. Now taking into account the definition of $e^\varepsilon_{i_0}$, we see that we get $$\displaystyle{I^\varepsilon = -\sigma + e^\varepsilon_{i_0} +(W''(\tilde{\phi}_{i_0})-W''(0))\left\{\tilde{\sigma} + \sum_{i\not= i_0} \frac{\tilde{\phi}_i}{\varepsilon} + \eta \overline{c}_{i_0}\right\} + W''(0) \tilde{\sigma}}$$ and then $$\displaystyle{I^\varepsilon = e^\varepsilon_{i_0} +(\alpha \tilde{\sigma} -\sigma) + O(\tilde{\phi}_{i_0})\left\{\tilde{\sigma} + \sum_{i\not= i_0} \frac{\tilde{\phi}_i}{\varepsilon} + \eta \overline{c}_{i_0}\right\}}.$$ This ends the proof of the lemma. \qed

nodes.name: Supersolution for positive time
nodes.statement: {\bf (Supersolution for positive time)}\\ Under assumption (A), there exists $\delta_0>0$ such that for all $0<\delta\le \delta_0$ and given $T>0$, we have \begin{equation} \overline{v}^\varepsilon_t \ge \frac{1}{\varepsilon} \left(L\overline{v}^\varepsilon - \frac{1}{\varepsilon} W'(\overline{v}^\varepsilon) +\sigma(t,x) \right) \quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R} \end{equation} for $\varepsilon >0$ small enough.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement:
oindent { f Proof of Theorem ef{th::1}}\ 
oindent { f Step 1: existence and uniqueness of the solution}\ First remark that for $\varepsilon$ small enough the initial condition satisfies $$-1\le v^\varepsilon_0 \le N+1$$ and the functions $$\underline{u}(t,x)=-1-K^\varepsilon t \quad \mbox{and}\quad \overline{u}(t,x)=N+1+K^\varepsilon t$$ with $$K^\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{-1}|\sigma|_{L^\infty([0,+\infty)	imes \hbox{ f R})} +\varepsilon^{-2} |W'|_{L^\infty(\hbox{ f R})}$$ are respectively sub and supersolutions of (ef{eq::1}) on $[0,+\infty)	imes \hbox{ f R}$. From the Perron's method, it follows the existence of a solution $v^\varepsilon$ of (ef{eq::1}) on $[0,+\infty)	imes \hbox{ f R}$ which is moreover unique thanks to the comparison principle (Proposition ef{pro:4}).\ 
oindent { f Step 2: sub and supersolutions as $\varepsilon 	o 0$}\ Now, given any fixed $T>0$, and thanks to Propositions ef{pro::2} and ef{pro::3}, we can find some $\delta>0$ small enough such that $\overline{v}^\varepsilon$ is a supersolution of (ef{eq::1}) on $[0,T)	imes \hbox{ f R}$.\ Similarly we can build a subsolution $\underline{v}^\varepsilon$ (defined simply as $\overline{v}^\varepsilon$ but with $\delta <0$). At the initial time we have $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x) \ge v^\varepsilon(0,x) \ge \underline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\hbox{ f R}$$ and then from the comparison principle, we get that $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(t,x) \ge v^\varepsilon(t,x) \ge \underline{v}^\varepsilon(t,x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad t\in [0,T),\quad x\in\hbox{ f R}.$$ Now for fixed $T>0$, we get the result (namely (ef{eq::c+}) and (ef{eq::c-})) on $[0,T)	imes \hbox{ f R}$, passing to the limit as $\varepsilon	o 0$. Finally, because $T>0$ was arbitrary, we recover the result for all time on $[0,+\infty)	imes \hbox{ f R}$. This ends the proof of the Theorem.\qed

nodes.statement_short: Perron's method plus comparison give existence and uniqueness; then explicit sub/supersolutions from Propositions 4.1 and 4.3 squeeze $v^\varepsilon$ as $\varepsilon\to0$.

nodes.name: Step 1: existence and uniqueness
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf Step 1: existence and uniqueness of the solution}\\ First remark that for $\varepsilon$ small enough the initial condition satisfies $$-1\le v^\varepsilon_0 \le N+1$$ and the functions $$\underline{u}(t,x)=-1-K^\varepsilon t \quad \mbox{and}\quad \overline{u}(t,x)=N+1+K^\varepsilon t$$ with $$K^\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{-1}|\sigma|_{L^\infty([0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R})} +\varepsilon^{-2} |W'|_{L^\infty(\hbox{\bf R})}$$ are respectively sub and supersolutions of (\ref{eq::1}) on $[0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}$. From the Perron's method, it follows the existence of a solution $v^\varepsilon$ of (\ref{eq::1}) on $[0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}$ which is moreover unique thanks to the comparison principle (Proposition \ref{pro:4}).\\
nodes.statement_short: Constant-slope barriers, Perron's method and comparison give a unique solution.

nodes.name: Step 2: sub and supersolutions as epsilon to 0
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf Step 2: sub and supersolutions as $\varepsilon \to 0$}\\ Now, given any fixed $T>0$, and thanks to Propositions \ref{pro::2} and \ref{pro::3}, we can find some $\delta>0$ small enough such that $\overline{v}^\varepsilon$ is a supersolution of (\ref{eq::1}) on $[0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}$.\\ Similarly we can build a subsolution $\underline{v}^\varepsilon$ (defined simply as $\overline{v}^\varepsilon$ but with $\delta <0$). At the initial time we have $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x) \ge v^\varepsilon(0,x) \ge \underline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}$$ and then from the comparison principle, we get that $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(t,x) \ge v^\varepsilon(t,x) \ge \underline{v}^\varepsilon(t,x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad t\in [0,T),\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}.$$ Now for fixed $T>0$, we get the result (namely (\ref{eq::c+}) and (\ref{eq::c-})) on $[0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}$, passing to the limit as $\varepsilon\to 0$. Finally, because $T>0$ was arbitrary, we recover the result for all time on $[0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}$. This ends the proof of the Theorem.\qed
nodes.statement_short: Squeeze $v^\varepsilon$ between the ansatz-based barriers and pass to the limit.

nodes.name: Supersolution from Propositions 4.1 and 4.3

nodes.name: Subsolution and comparison
nodes.statement: Similarly we can build a subsolution $\underline{v}^\varepsilon$ (defined simply as $\overline{v}^\varepsilon$ but with $\delta <0$). At the initial time we have $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x) \ge v^\varepsilon(0,x) \ge \underline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}$$ and then from the comparison principle, we get that $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(t,x) \ge v^\varepsilon(t,x) \ge \underline{v}^\varepsilon(t,x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad t\in [0,T),\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}.$$

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: Now for fixed $T>0$, we get the result (namely (\ref{eq::c+}) and (\ref{eq::c-})) on $[0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}$, passing to the limit as $\varepsilon\to 0$. Finally, because $T>0$ was arbitrary, we recover the result for all time on $[0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}$. This ends the proof of the Theorem.\qed

nodes.name: Fourier transform and the space $H^{1/2}$
nodes.statement: We recall our definition of the Fourier transform for $w \in {\mathcal S}(\hbox{\bf R})$ (where ${\mathcal S}(\hbox{\bf R})$ is the Schwartz space): $$\widehat{w}(\xi)=\int_{\hbox{\bf R}}w(x) \ e^{-i\xi x}dx \quad \mbox{for all}\quad \xi\in\hbox{\bf R}$$ and recall the definition of the following Hilbert space $$H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})=\left\{w\in L^2(\hbox{\bf R}),\quad \int_{\hbox{\bf R}}d\xi\ (1+|\xi|)|\widehat{w}(\xi)|^2 < +\infty \right\}$$ with the scalar product $$(v,w)_{H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})}=\int_{\hbox{\bf R}}d\xi\ (1+|\xi|)\widehat{v}^*(\xi) \widehat{w}(\xi)$$ where $\widehat{v}^*$ denotes here the complex conjugate of $\widehat{v}$.
nodes.statement_short: Fourier transform on Schwartz space and the Hilbert space $H^{1/2}$ with weight $1+|\xi|$.

nodes.name: The space $H^{-1/2}$
nodes.statement: We also set the following Hilbert space $$H^{-\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})=\left\{w\in {\mathcal S}'(\hbox{\bf R}),\quad \widehat{w}\in L^2_{loc}(\hbox{\bf R}),\quad \int_{\hbox{\bf R}}d\xi\ (1+|\xi|)^{-1}|\widehat{w}(\xi)|^2 < +\infty \right\}$$ with the scalar product $$(v,w)_{H^{-\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})}=\int_{\hbox{\bf R}}d\xi\ (1+|\xi|)^{-1}\widehat{v}^*(\xi) \widehat{w}(\xi).$$

nodes.name: Duality of H^{1/2} and H^{-1/2}
nodes.statement: It is known that $H^{-\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$ is the dual of $H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$.
conclusions: It is known that $H^{-\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$ is the dual of $H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$.

nodes.name: Half-Laplacian in Fourier space
nodes.statement: Recall that we set $L=-(-\Delta)^{\frac12}$ to be the half-Laplacian operator defined in Fourier space by \begin{equation} \widehat{Lw}(\xi):=-|\xi|\widehat{w}(\xi) \quad \mbox{for}\quad \xi\in\hbox{\bf R}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Fourier symbol of the half-Laplacian
nodes.statement: \widehat{Lw}(\xi):=-|\xi|\widehat{w}(\xi) \quad \mbox{for}\quad \xi\in\hbox{\bf R}.
nodes.label: eq::3

nodes.name: Continuity of L from H^{1/2} to H^{-1/2}
nodes.statement: In particular, $L$ is a continuous linear mapping from $H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$ into $H^{-\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$ satisfying $$\norm{Lw}_{H^{-\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})}\le \norm{w}_{H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})}.$$
conclusions: $L$ is a continuous linear mapping from $H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$ into $H^{-\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$ satisfying $$\norm{Lw}_{H^{-\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})}\le \norm{w}_{H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})}.$$

nodes.name: Self-adjointness of L
nodes.statement: Moreover $L$ is self-adjoint as follows: for any $v,w \in H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$, we have $$<Lv,w>_{H^{-\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})\times H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})}= <Lw,v>_{H^{-\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})\times H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})}.$$
conclusions: $L$ is self-adjoint

nodes.name: The Levy-Khintchine formula
nodes.statement: {\bf (The L\'evy-Khintchine formula)}\\ For any $0<\beta<1$, if $w\in H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})\cap C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\hbox{\bf R})$, then we have $$Lw(x)=\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{\hbox{\bf R}}\frac{dz}{z^2}\left(w(x+z)-w(x)-zw'(x) 1_{\left\{|z|\le 1\right\}}\right).$$ Moreover this formula allows also to define $Lw$ for instance for $w\in L^\infty(\hbox{\bf R})\cap C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\hbox{\bf R})$.

nodes.name: Truncation radius in the Levy-Khintchine formula
nodes.statement: In the previous formula the characteristic function $1_{\left\{|z|\le 1\right\}}$ can be replaced by $1_{\left\{|z|\le r\right\}}$ for any $r>0$, which does not change the value of the integral.

nodes.name: Weak sub/super/solution
nodes.statement: {\bf (Weak sub/super/solution)}\\ Let $d$ be a measurable bounded function on $\mathbb R$, and let $g\in L^2(\mathbb R)$. We say that $w\in H^\frac{1}{2}(\mathbb R)$ is a weak supersolution for the equation \begin{equation} Lw -d(x)w=g \quad \mbox{ on }\partial\Omega \end{equation} if, for $u:=P*_x w$ and $$B(u,v):=\int_{\Omega}\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+\int_{\partial\Omega} d(x)(Tu)(Tv),$$ we have that \begin{equation}B(u,v)\geq \int_{\partial\Omega} gTv\quad\mbox{for all }v\in H.\end{equation} Respectively, $w$ is a weak subsolution if \begin{equation} B(u,v)\leq \int_{\partial\Omega} gTv\quad\mbox{for all }v\in H.\end{equation} Accordingly, we say that $w$ is a weak solution if it is both a weak sub and supersolution.\\

nodes.name: Layer solution of the boundary reaction problem

nodes.name: Known existence and properties of the layer solution
nodes.statement: {\bf (Known existence and properties of the layer solution)}\\ Let $f$ be any $\mathcal C^{1,\beta}$ function with $0 < \beta < 1$ and such that $W'= -f$. Then there exists a layer solution $u_W\in \mathcal C^{2,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\overline\Omega)$ of \eqref{Cabre-SolaMorales-layer} if and only if $$W'(0)=W'(1)=0\quad\mbox{and}\quad W> W(0)=W(1)\quad\mbox{in } (0,1).$$ Moreover, \begin{enumerate} \item If $W''(0), W''(1)>0$, then a layer solution of \eqref{Cabre-SolaMorales-layer} is unique up to translations in the $x$ variable, and it satisfies \begin{equation}(u_W)_x>0\quad\mbox{in }\overline{\Omega}.\end{equation} \item We have the estimate \begin{equation}\abs{\nabla u_W(x,y)}\leq \frac{C}{1+\abs{(x,y)}}, \quad \mbox{for all }x\in\mathbb R, y\geq 0.\end{equation} \item Set $\phi(x):=u_W(x,0)$. We have the bounds \begin{equation} \abs{\phi(x)-H(x)}\leq \frac{C}{1+\abs{x}} \quad\mbox{for all }x\in\mathbb R, \end{equation} \begin{equation} \frac{C_1}{1+\abs{x}^2} \leq \phi'(x)\leq \frac{C_2}{1+\abs{x}^2},\quad \mbox{for all }x\in\mathbb R, \end{equation} for some positive constants $C,C_1,C_2$. \item A layer solution is always a stable solution. This means that \begin{equation}\int_{\Omega}\abs{\nabla v}^2+\int_{\partial\Omega}W''(\phi)v^2\geq 0\end{equation} for every function $v\in\mathcal C^1(\overline{\Omega})$ with compact support in $\overline{\Omega}$.\\ \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $f$ be any $\mathcal C^{1,\beta}$ function with $0 < \beta < 1$ and such that $W'= -f$
conclusions: Then there exists a layer solution $u_W\in \mathcal C^{2,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\overline\Omega)$ of \eqref{Cabre-SolaMorales-layer} if and only if $$W'(0)=W'(1)=0\quad\mbox{and}\quad W> W(0)=W(1)\quad\mbox{in } (0,1).$$

If $W''(0), W''(1)>0$, then a layer solution of \eqref{Cabre-SolaMorales-layer} is unique up to translations in the $x$ variable, and it satisfies \begin{equation}(u_W)_x>0\quad\mbox{in }\overline{\Omega}.\end{equation}
We have the estimate \begin{equation}\abs{\nabla u_W(x,y)}\leq \frac{C}{1+\abs{(x,y)}}, \quad \mbox{for all }x\in\mathbb R, y\geq 0.\end{equation}
A layer solution is always a stable solution.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.14
nodes.statement: This is a small variation of the classical proof for the Laplacian, that can be found in Gilbarg-Trudinger \cite{Gilbarg-Trudinger}, Theorem 8.1. Note that $(Tu)^-= T(u^-)$ a.e. in $\mathbb R$. Set $$\Omega^-:=supp (u^-)\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Theta:=supp((Tu)^-)\subset \mathbb R.$$ We know that $\Omega^-$ is contained in $\mathbb R^2_+\backslash B_R^+$ and $\Theta\subset \mathbb R\backslash(-R,R)$. Use $u^-\in H$ as an admissible test function in \eqref{weak-super-solution}; then $$0\leq -\int_{\Omega^-} \abs{\nabla u}^2-\int_{\Theta}d(x)u^2.$$ The proof is easily completed.

Then $$\sup_{\mathbb R} w\leq C \norm{w^+}_{L^2(\mathbb R)}.$$ If $w$ is a supersolution, the conclusion reads $$\sup_{\mathbb R} \{-w\}\leq C \norm{w^-}_{L^2(\mathbb R)}.$$ The constant does not depend on $w$. nodes.name: Follow Moser's proof
nodes.statement: This is the classical proof by Moser for the Laplacian case. We follow closely the arguments from Theorems 8.15 and 8.18 in Gilbarg-Trudinger \cite{Gilbarg-Trudinger}, so we will not give every single detail here.

nodes.name: Power test function
nodes.statement: Assume that $w$ is a subsolution, and set $u:=P*_x w$. Given $\sigma\ge 1$, we insert into \eqref{weak-sub-solution}, the test function $$v=(u^+)^\sigma.$$ Note that $Tv=(Tu)^\sigma$ a.e.. Here we point out that this $v$ might not belong to $H$; in order to make the argument rigorous, a truncated version must be used instead in the definition of $v$, say replacing $u^+$ by \begin{equation} \min\{u^+,n\},\quad \mbox{for}\quad n\in \mathbb N. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Energy estimate

nodes.name: Trace and Sobolev inequalities
nodes.statement: For the left hand side, we proceed as follows. We use the trace inequality \eqref{trace-inequality} to estimate $$\frac{1}{2\pi}\norm{w_1}^2_{\dot H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)} \le \int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u_1}^2.$$ But, on the other hand, by Theorem \ref{Sobolev}, for every $p>1$, there exists a constant $C_p>0$ such that $$\begin{array}{ll} ||w_1||^2_{L^{2p}}&\le C_p\left(||w_1||^2_{L^2}+||w_1||^2_{\dot{H}^{\frac12}}\right)\\ \\ &\le C_2(\gamma) ||w_1||^2_{L^2} \quad \mbox{with}\quad C_2(\gamma)=C_p(1+2\pi C_1(\gamma)), \end{array}$$ where we have used \eqref{moser-1} in the last line.\\
nodes.statement_short: Trace inequality and Sobolev embedding give an $L^{2p}$ bound for $w_1$.

nodes.name: Iteration
nodes.statement: If we denote $$\Psi (q):=\left(\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{w^+}^{q}\right)^{\frac{1}{q}},$$ then we have shown that $$\Psi(2p\gamma)\leq \left[C_2(\gamma)\right]^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}}\Psi(2\gamma).$$ Fixed $p>1$ and choose $\gamma_m=p^m$ for $m\in\hbox{\bf N}$; by iteration we know \begin{equation} \Psi(2\gamma_m)\leq C_m\Psi(2),\quad \forall m\in\mathbb N\backslash\left\{0\right\},\quad C_m:=\prod_{j=0}^{m-1} \left[C_2(\gamma_j)\right]^\frac{1}{2\gamma_j}.\end{equation} It is then easy to check that $C_m\le C_\infty$ uniformly bounded in $m\in\mathbb N$ (which is also shown, for instance, in page 190 of \cite{Gilbarg-Trudinger}).
nodes.statement_short: Iterate with $\gamma_m=p^m$ to bound $\Psi(2\gamma_m)$ uniformly.

We get the first part of the conclusion, taking $R\to +\infty$ and then $n\to +\infty$ in (\ref{eq::902}).
nodes.statement_short: Let $m\to\infty$, then $R\to\infty$ and $n\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.16
nodes.statement: We use Proposition \ref{prop-moser-iteration} with some modifications in order to account for the extra right hand side term involving $g$. By hypothesis, $w$ is a weak solution satisfying for all $v\in H$, $$B(u,v)=-\int_{\partial\Omega} gv, \quad\mbox{for }u=P*_x w.$$ Similarly as before (using if necessary a truncated version), we use the test function $v=\abs{u}^{\sigma-1} u$, $u_1=|u|^{\gamma-1}u$ and $w_1 = Tu_1$. We use H\"older inequality with exponents $2\gamma$, $\frac{2\gamma}{2\gamma-1}$, which gives $$\abs{\int_{\partial\Omega} gv}\leq \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{g}^{2\gamma}\right)^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}} \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2}\right)^{\frac{2\gamma-1}{2\gamma}},$$ we get \begin{equation*}\begin{split} \int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u_1}^2 &\le C_1(\gamma) \int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2} +\tilde{C}_1(\gamma)\left(\int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2}\right)^{\frac{2\gamma-1}{2\gamma}}\quad \mbox{with}\quad \tilde{C}_1(\gamma)= \frac{\gamma^2}{2\gamma-1}\cdot \left(\int_{\partial \Omega} |g|^{2\gamma}\right)^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}}. \end{split}\end{equation*} Assuming (\ref{eq::904}) with $2\gamma\ge p_0$, we get $$\int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u_1}^2 \le \bar{C}_1(\gamma) \max\left\{1,\int_{\partial \Omega} w_1^2\right\} \quad \mbox{with}\quad \bar{C}_1(\gamma) = C_1(\gamma) + \frac{c\gamma^2}{2\gamma-1}$$ The rest of the argument follows similarly, with $\bar{C}_2(\gamma)=\max\left\{1,C_p(1+2\pi \bar{C}_1(\gamma))\right\}$, $\bar\Psi(q)=\max \left\{1,\left(\int_{\partial\Omega}|w|^q\right)^{\frac1q}\right\}$, and $\bar \Psi(2p\gamma)\le (\bar C_2(\gamma))^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}}\bar \Psi(2\gamma)$, starting the iteration at $2\gamma=p_0$.\qed\\

nodes.name: Iterate

Let $W$ be a potential satisfying hypothesis \emph{Ai)}. Theorem ef{thm-layer-solutions} shows existence, regularity, uniqueness and asymptotic behavior of a layer solution $0<u_W<1$ satisfying $u_W(0,0)=1/2$, $u\in\mathcal C^{2, eta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\overline{\Omega})$, for the problem  egin{equation} \left\{ egin{split} \Delta u &= 0 &\quad \mbox{in } \Omega,\  rac{\partial u}{\partial 
u} &= -W'(u) &\quad \mbox{on } \partial\Omega. \end{split}ight.\end{equation} We denote its trace value by $\phi:=u_W(\cdot,0)$. The aim of the next paragraphs is to show the more precise estimate \eqref{eq::6} for the asymptotic behavior near infinity.\ Set $a=1/\alpha$, where $\alpha=W''(0)$ as defined in (ef{eq::900}), and choose the model layer solution $u^a$ as given in \eqref{model-layer}. We know explicitly because of \eqref{asymptotic-layer} that $\phi^a:=u^a(\cdot,0)$ has the right asymptotic behavior \eqref{eq::6}. We would like to compare $u_W$ to $u^a$, in order to obtain the analogous estimate for $u_W$. Therefore, we set $v:=u_W-u^a$. Then $v$ satisfies  egin{equation*}\left\{ egin{split} &\Delta v= \;0 \quad &\mbox{in } \Omega,\ & rac{\partial v}{\partial 
u}= -W'(\phi)+V'_a(\phi^a)\quad &\mbox{on } \partial\Omega. \end{split}ight. \end{equation*} Now we estimate $$-W'(\phi)+W'(\phi^a)=-W''(0)[\phi-\phi^a]+O\left(  rac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}ight),$$ thanks to the growth estimate \eqref{growth-not-sharp}. And also, $$-W'(\phi^a)+V'_a(\phi^a)=[-W''(0)+V_a''(0)]\phi^a+O\left(  rac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}ight).$$ Because of the choice of $a$, we have that $W''(0)=V_a''(0)$. Thus adding the previous two lines we conclude that $v$ is a solution of  egin{equation*}\left\{ egin{split} &\Delta v = 0 \quad &\mbox{ in } \Omega,\ & rac{\partial v}{\partial 
u} +W''(0) v=M(x) &\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega, \end{split}ight.\end{equation*} for some function $M$ satisfying $$\abs{M(x)}=O\left(  rac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}ight) .$$ Therefore, \eqref{eq::6} follows from Corollary ef{cor-comparison} (comparison principle for smooth solutions) and the fact that $W''(0)>0$. The proof of Theorem ef{th::5} is completed due to the fact that a smooth, bounded solution $u$ of \eqref{smooth-solution}, with trace $\phi$, is a viscosity solution in the sense of Definition ef{defi::1} of $$L \phi -W'(\phi)=0\quad \mbox{in }\mathbb R,$$ with $L$ defined through the L'evy-Khintchine formula, as it is noted in Lemma ef{lemma-equivalence}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Compare the layer with the explicit Peierls-Nabarro layer $u^a$, $a=1/\alpha$: the difference solves a Robin problem with $O(1/x^2)$ data, so Corollary 5.13 gives the sharp asymptotics.

nodes.name: Boundary reaction problem for u_W
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{split} \Delta u &= 0 &\quad \mbox{in } \Omega,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu} &= -W'(u) &\quad \mbox{on } \partial\Omega. \end{split}\right.
nodes.label: smooth-solution

nodes.name: Layer from Cabre-Sola-Morales
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be a potential satisfying hypothesis \emph{Ai)}. Theorem \ref{thm-layer-solutions} shows existence, regularity, uniqueness and asymptotic behavior of a layer solution $0<u_W<1$ satisfying $u_W(0,0)=1/2$, $u\in\mathcal C^{2,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\overline{\Omega})$, for the problem \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{split} \Delta u &= 0 &\quad \mbox{in } \Omega,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu} &= -W'(u) &\quad \mbox{on } \partial\Omega. \end{split}\right.\end{equation} We denote its trace value by $\phi:=u_W(\cdot,0)$. The aim of the next paragraphs is to show the more precise estimate \eqref{eq::6} for the asymptotic behavior near infinity.\\
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 5.10 gives the layer $u_W$ with trace $\phi$.

nodes.name: Compare with model layer
nodes.statement: Set $a=1/\alpha$, where $\alpha=W''(0)$ as defined in (\ref{eq::900}), and choose the model layer solution $u^a$ as given in \eqref{model-layer}. We know explicitly because of \eqref{asymptotic-layer} that $\phi^a:=u^a(\cdot,0)$ has the right asymptotic behavior \eqref{eq::6}. We would like to compare $u_W$ to $u^a$, in order to obtain the analogous estimate for $u_W$. Therefore, we set $v:=u_W-u^a$. Then $v$ satisfies \begin{equation*}\left\{\begin{split} &\Delta v= \;0 \quad &\mbox{in } \Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial \nu}= -W'(\phi)+V'_a(\phi^a)\quad &\mbox{on } \partial\Omega. \end{split}\right. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Set $v=u_W-u^a$ with $a=1/\alpha$; $v$ is harmonic with Neumann data $-W'(\phi)+V_a'(\phi^a)$.

nodes.name: Linearize the boundary data
nodes.statement: Now we estimate $$-W'(\phi)+W'(\phi^a)=-W''(0)[\phi-\phi^a]+O\left( \frac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}\right),$$ thanks to the growth estimate \eqref{growth-not-sharp}. And also, $$-W'(\phi^a)+V'_a(\phi^a)=[-W''(0)+V_a''(0)]\phi^a+O\left( \frac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}\right).$$ Because of the choice of $a$, we have that $W''(0)=V_a''(0)$. Thus adding the previous two lines we conclude that $v$ is a solution of \begin{equation*}\left\{\begin{split} &\Delta v = 0 \quad &\mbox{ in } \Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial \nu} +W''(0) v=M(x) &\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega, \end{split}\right.\end{equation*} for some function $M$ satisfying $$\abs{M(x)}=O\left( \frac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}\right) .$$
nodes.statement_short: Taylor expansion shows $\partial_\nu v+W''(0)v=O(1/(1+x^2))$.

nodes.name: Apply Corollary 5.13
nodes.statement: Therefore, \eqref{eq::6} follows from Corollary \ref{cor-comparison} (comparison principle for smooth solutions) and the fact that $W''(0)>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Corollary 5.13 yields (17).

nodes.name: Viscosity sense
nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem \ref{th::5} is completed due to the fact that a smooth, bounded solution $u$ of \eqref{smooth-solution}, with trace $\phi$, is a viscosity solution in the sense of Definition \ref{defi::1} of $$L \phi -W'(\phi)=0\quad \mbox{in }\mathbb R,$$ with $L$ defined through the L\'evy-Khintchine formula, as it is noted in Lemma \ref{lemma-equivalence}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Smooth solutions are viscosity solutions by Lemma 5.6.

nodes.name: Asymptotics of phi and phi'
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{split} \left|\phi(x)-H(x)+\frac{1}{\alpha \pi x}\right| \quad &\le \quad \frac{C}{1+x^2}, \\ \abs{\phi'(x)} &\leq \frac{C}{1+x^2}, \end{split}\right.
nodes.label: asymptotics

nodes.name: Subspace $H_0$
nodes.statement: We set $H_0$ to be the subspace in $H$ consisting of functions whose trace is orthogonal to $\phi'$ in $L^2(\partial\Omega)$, i.e, \begin{equation} H_0:=\left\{ u\in H : \int_{\partial\Omega} u\phi'=0\right\}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Definition of H_0
nodes.statement: H_0:=\left\{ u\in H : \int_{\partial\Omega} u\phi'=0\right\}.
nodes.label: space

nodes.name: H_0 is closed
nodes.statement: $H_0$ is a closed subspace of $H$.
conclusions: $H_0$ is a closed subspace of $H$.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: As we have noted in Theorem \ref{th::3}, the trace of functions in $H$ is a well defined function in $H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$. In particular, the trace mapping $T:H\to L^2(\mathbb R)$ is continuous by Sobolev embedding (Theorem \ref{Sobolev}). Then, if we have a sequence $\{u_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\to u_0$ in $H$ with $u_k\in H_0$, then $$\abs{\int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'(u_k-u_0)}\leq \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{u_k-u_0}^2\right)^{1/2}\to 0\quad\mbox{when } k\to \infty,$$ using the bounds for $\phi'$ given in \eqref{asymptotics}. We conclude that $u_0\in H_0$, and the lemma is shown.
nodes.statement_short: The trace map into $L^2$ is continuous, so the orthogonality constraint passes to limits by Cauchy-Schwarz.

nodes.name: Continuity of the trace into L^2
nodes.statement: As we have noted in Theorem \ref{th::3}, the trace of functions in $H$ is a well defined function in $H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$. In particular, the trace mapping $T:H\to L^2(\mathbb R)$ is continuous by Sobolev embedding (Theorem \ref{Sobolev}).
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 5.3 and Sobolev embedding make $T:H\to L^2$ continuous.

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: Then, if we have a sequence $\{u_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\to u_0$ in $H$ with $u_k\in H_0$, then $$\abs{\int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'(u_k-u_0)}\leq \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{u_k-u_0}^2\right)^{1/2}\to 0\quad\mbox{when } k\to \infty,$$ using the bounds for $\phi'$ given in \eqref{asymptotics}.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz shows the constraint passes to the limit.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: We conclude that $u_0\in H_0$, and the lemma is shown.
nodes.statement_short: The limit lies in $H_0$.

nodes.name: Bilinear form B and quadratic form Q
nodes.statement:
Now, given $u,v\in H$, we define the bilinear functional  egin{equation} B(u,v):=\int_\Omega 
abla u \cdot
abla v+\int_{\partial\Omega} W''(\phi)uv,\end{equation} whose associated quadratic form is precisely $$Q(u)=\int_\Omega|
abla u|^2+\int_{\partial\Omega}W''(\phi)u^2,\quad u\in H.$$

nodes.name: Bilinear functional
nodes.statement: B(u,v):=\int_\Omega \nabla u \cdot\nabla v+\int_{\partial\Omega} W''(\phi)uv,
nodes.label: bilinear-functional

nodes.name: B is continuous and symmetric
nodes.statement: It is easy to check that $B$ is a continuous and symmetric bilinear functional in $H$.
conclusions: $B$ is a continuous and symmetric bilinear functional in $H$

nodes.name: Lower bound for Q
nodes.statement: {\bf (Lower bound for $Q$).} There is some constant $C_0>0$ such that for all $u\in H_0$, where $H_0$ is defined in \eqref{space}, we have that $$Q(u)\geq C_0\int_{\partial\Omega} u^2.$$
conclusions: $$Q(u)\geq C_0\int_{\partial\Omega} u^2.$$
nodes.statement_short: $Q$ controls the boundary $L^2$ norm on functions whose trace is orthogonal to $\phi'$.
nodes.label: lem:1

nodes.name: Coercivity
nodes.statement: {\bf (Coercivity).} There exists some $C>0$ such that for all $u\in H_0$, $$B(u,u)\geq C\norm{u}_H^2.$$
conclusions: $$B(u,u)\geq C\norm{u}_H^2.$$
nodes.label: cor-coercivity

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 6.3
nodes.statement_short: Interpolate between Lemma 6.2 and $Q$ itself with a small weight $\mu$.

nodes.name: Coercivity constant
nodes.statement: B(u,u)\geq\min\left\{\mu,\tfrac{C_0}{2}\right\} \norm{u}_H^2,
nodes.label: eq::909

nodes.name: Interpolate with Lemma 6.2
nodes.statement: It easily follows from Lemma \ref{lem:1}. Indeed, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} B(u,u) & =\int_\Omega \abs{\nabla u}^2+\int_{\partial\Omega}W''(\phi)u^2\geq (1-\mu) C_0 \int_{\partial\Omega} u^2+\mu Q(u)\\ & \geq \mu\int_\Omega \abs{\nabla u}^2+\int_{\partial\Omega} u^2\left[(1-\mu)C_0+\mu W''(\phi)\right].\\ \end{split}\end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Split $B(u,u)$ as $(1-\mu)$ times the Lemma 6.2 bound plus $\mu Q(u)$.

nodes.name: Choose mu
nodes.statement: Because $W''$ is bounded, there exists $\mu>0$ small enough such that $(1-\mu)C_0+\mu W''(\phi)>\tfrac{C_0}{2}$. Therefore, \begin{equation} B(u,u)\geq\min\left\{\mu,\tfrac{C_0}{2}\right\} \norm{u}_H^2, \end{equation} as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Small $\mu$ gives (58).

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.2
nodes.statement_short: Direct method: minimize $Q$ on the $L^2$-unit sphere of $H_0$, using stability, compact embedding and weak lower semicontinuity. A comparison argument with $\bar u=\partial_x u_W$ excludes a zero minimum value.

nodes.name: Harmonic extension lowers Q_1
nodes.statement: Q_1(\tilde u_k)\leq Q_1(u_k)
nodes.label: Q_1

nodes.name: Lower semicontinuity of Q_1
nodes.statement: Q_1(u_0)=\norm{w_0}_{\tilde H}\leq \liminf_{k\to\infty} \norm{w_k}_{\tilde H}=Q_1(\tilde u_k)\leq Q_1(u_k).
nodes.label: Q1

nodes.name: Zero infimum assumption
nodes.statement: \liminf Q(u_k) =0
nodes.label: eq::910

nodes.name: Convergence of Q_1
nodes.statement: Q_1(\tilde u_k) \to \ Q_1(u_0).
nodes.label: limit1

nodes.name: Convergence of norms
nodes.statement: \lim_{k\to\infty} \norm{w_k}_{\tilde H}=\norm{w_0}_{\tilde H}.
nodes.label: norms-are-equal

nodes.name: Euler-Lagrange equation with multipliers
nodes.statement: B(u_0,v)=\lambda \int_{\partial\Omega} u_0v+\mu \int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'v \quad \mbox{ for every } v\in H,
nodes.label: Lagrange

nodes.name: Value of the multiplier
nodes.statement: \lambda=Q(u_0)=\int_{\Omega}\abs{\nabla u_0}^2+\int_{\partial\Omega} W''(\phi)u_0^2 \quad (\geq 0).
nodes.label: eq::100

nodes.name: First touching point
nodes.statement: \kappa^* \bar u=u_0 \quad \mbox{at }(x_0,y_0)\quad \mbox{and}\quad \kappa^*\bar u \ge u_0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad \overline{\Omega}.
nodes.label: functions-touch

nodes.name: Positive lower bound C_0
nodes.statement: Q(u)\geq Q(u_0)=\lambda=: C_0>0 \quad\mbox{for all }u\in H_0 \mbox{ with }\int_{\partial\Omega} u^2=1.
nodes.label: eq:100

nodes.name: Outline
nodes.statement: \textbf{Proof of Lemma \ref{lem:1}:} It is divided into several steps:\\
nodes.statement_short: The proof is in steps.

nodes.name: Step 1: Stability
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 1: Stability.} Because of the construction of $u_W$ and $\phi$, we know from Theorem \ref{thm-layer-solutions} that $Q(u)\geq 0$ for all $u\in \mathcal C_c^\infty(\bar\Omega)$ (i.e. layer solutions are stable). Thus the functional $Q$ is bounded from below also in $H$.\\
nodes.statement_short: Stability of layers (Theorem 5.10) gives $Q\ge0$.

nodes.name: Step 2: Existence of a minimizer
nodes.statement_short: Existence of a constrained minimizer of $Q$.

nodes.name: Step 2.1: Preliminaries
nodes.statement_short: Bounded minimizing sequence, weak limit $u_0$ with $Q(u_0)\le\liminf Q(u_k)$; reduce to $\liminf Q(u_k)=0$.

nodes.name: Step 2.2: Concluding
nodes.statement:
\emph{Step 2.2: Concluding.}\ \emph{Case A: $u_0\equiv 0$}\ Remark first that $$Q_1(u_k)\ge 	au \int_{\partial \Omega} u_k^2 = 	au >0.$$ On the other hand, we have $Q_2(u_k)	o Q_2(u_0)=0$. Therefore we get $$\liminf_{k	o\infty} Q(u_k) = \liminf_{k	o\infty} \left\{Q_1(u_k)+ Q_2(u_k)ight\} \ge 	au >0,$$ which is in contradiction with (ef{eq::910}). Therefore only the next case occurs.\ \emph{Case B: $u_0
ot\equiv 0$}\ Then we have $0\le Q_1(u_0)=0$ and we will show that $Tu_k	o T u_0$ in $H^ rac{1}{2}(\mathbb R)$. Since $\{u_k\}$ was a minimizing sequence, then $Q(u_k)	o 0= Q(u_0)$ when $k	o\infty$. In addition, we have shown that $Tu_k	o Tu_0$ strongly in $L^2(K)$, so that $Q_2(u_k)	o Q_2(u_0)$. Because $Q(u_0)=0\le Q(	ilde{u}_k)\le Q(u_k) 	o 0$, we deduce that $Q(	ilde{u}_k)	o Q(u_0)$. Moreover we have $Q_2(	ilde{u}_k)= Q_2(u_k) 	o Q_2(u_0)$ and $Q=Q_1+Q_2$ which implies that  egin{equation} Q_1(	ilde u_k) 	o \ Q_1(u_0).\end{equation} By definition \eqref{limit1} means that  egin{equation} \lim_{k	o\infty}

As a consequence, $w_k=Tu_k	o Tu_0=w_0$ in $L^2(\mathbb R)$, which, in particular, implies the non-degeneracy of the $L^2(\partial\Omega)$ norm of $w_0$: $$\int_{\partial\Omega}w_0^2=\lim_{k	o\infty}\int_{\partial\Omega} w_k^2 =1.$$ To finish, just remark that strong convergence in $L^2(\mathbb R)$ implies that $\int_{\partial\Omega} u_0 \phi'=0$. Thus, $u_0\in H_0$.\

nodes.name: Case A: u_0 = 0
nodes.statement: \emph{Case A: $u_0\equiv 0$}\\ Remark first that $$Q_1(u_k)\ge \tau \int_{\partial \Omega} u_k^2 = \tau >0.$$ On the other hand, we have $Q_2(u_k)\to Q_2(u_0)=0$. Therefore we get $$\liminf_{k\to\infty} Q(u_k) = \liminf_{k\to\infty} \left\{Q_1(u_k)+ Q_2(u_k)\right\} \ge \tau >0,$$ which is in contradiction with (\ref{eq::910}). Therefore only the next case occurs.\\
nodes.statement_short: If $u_0\equiv0$ then $\liminf Q(u_k)\ge\tau$, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Case B: u_0 nonzero
nodes.statement:
\emph{Case B: $u_0
ot\equiv 0$}\ Then we have $0\le Q_1(u_0)=0$ and we will show that $Tu_k	o T u_0$ in $H^ rac{1}{2}(\mathbb R)$. Since $\{u_k\}$ was a minimizing sequence, then $Q(u_k)	o 0= Q(u_0)$ when $k	o\infty$. In addition, we have shown that $Tu_k	o Tu_0$ strongly in $L^2(K)$, so that $Q_2(u_k)	o Q_2(u_0)$. Because $Q(u_0)=0\le Q(	ilde{u}_k)\le Q(u_k) 	o 0$, we deduce that $Q(	ilde{u}_k)	o Q(u_0)$. Moreover we have $Q_2(	ilde{u}_k)= Q_2(u_k) 	o Q_2(u_0)$ and $Q=Q_1+Q_2$ which implies that  egin{equation} Q_1(	ilde u_k) 	o \ Q_1(u_0).\end{equation} By definition \eqref{limit1} means that  egin{equation} \lim_{k	o\infty} 
orm{w_k}_{	ilde H}=
orm{w_0}_{	ilde H}.\end{equation} Proposition III.30 in \cite{Brezis:book} assures that if we have a weakly convergent sequence $w_kightharpoondown w_0$ in the space $	ilde H$ and such that we have convergence of the norms \eqref{norms-are-equal}, then the convergence $w_k	o w_0$ is strong in $	ilde H$, and then in $H^{ rac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$. As a consequence, $w_k=Tu_k	o Tu_0=w_0$ in $L^2(\mathbb R)$, which, in particular, implies the non-degeneracy of the $L^2(\partial\Omega)$ norm of $w_0$: $$\int_{\partial\Omega}w_0^2=\lim_{k	o\infty}\int_{\partial\Omega} w_k^2 =1.$$ To finish, just remark that strong convergence in $L^2(\mathbb R)$ implies that $\int_{\partial\Omega} u_0 \phi'=0$. Thus, $u_0\in H_0$.\

nodes.name: Step 3: Euler-Lagrange equation
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 3: Euler-Lagrange equation.} Once the minimizer $u_0$ is found, the theory of Lagrange multipliers for minimization problems (see, for instance, \cite{Evans}, chapter 8.4) gives that $u_0\in H$ must be a weak solution of \begin{equation} B(u_0,v)=\lambda \int_{\partial\Omega} u_0v+\mu \int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'v \quad \mbox{ for every } v\in H,\end{equation} where $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$. The value of the multipliers can be found by choosing the right test function $v$. Thus if we test the equality \eqref{Lagrange} with $v=P*_x\phi'$, we obtain $\mu=0$ (see Lemma \ref{properties}), while testing against $v=u_0$ gives that \begin{equation} \lambda=Q(u_0)=\int_{\Omega}\abs{\nabla u_0}^2+\int_{\partial\Omega} W''(\phi)u_0^2 \quad (\geq 0).\end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Lagrange multipliers: $\mu=0$ by Lemma 5.11 and $\lambda=Q(u_0)\ge0$.

nodes.name: Step 4: Regularity
nodes.statement:
\emph{Step 4: Regularity.} First, Proposition ef{prop-moser-iteration} with $d(x)=W''(\phi(x))-\lambda$ implies a uniform $L^\infty$ bound for both $w_0$ and $u_0=P*_x w_0$. Then, Proposition ef{prop-regularity} assures that $u_0\in\mathcal C^{1, eta}_{\mbox{loc}}( ar\Omega)$, with the following boundary estimate $$
orm{u_0}_{\mathcal C^{1, eta}(\overline{B_R^+})}\leq C\left(  eta,R,
orm{u_0}_{L^\infty(B_{4R}^+)}, 
orm{W''(\phi)}_{\mathcal C^{ eta}([-4R,4R])}ight).$$ Note that $u_0$ is as smooth as we want in the interior.
nodes.statement_short: Propositions 5.15 and 5.17 give boundedness and $C^{1,\beta}$ regularity of $u_0$.

nodes.name: Step 5: Positivity
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 5: Positivity.} In the following we show that if $\lambda=0$, then $w_0=Tu_0$ must necessarily be a multiple of $\phi'$, which is a contradiction with the fact that $u_0\in H_0$ and $\int_{\partial \Omega} u_0^2=1$. Thus we take $\lambda=0$ in \eqref{Lagrange}. Then we have a solution $u_0$ satisfying $B(u_0,v)=0$ for all $v\in H$. We remind the reader that have defined $u_W$ to be the layer solution for our potential $W$, with trace $\phi:=u_W(\cdot,0)$, and $\bar u:=\partial_x u_W$, which is also uniformly bounded and has trace $\bar u(\cdot, 0)=\phi'$. Because of the hypothesis on the potential $W$ and the asymptotic behavior of the layer solution $\phi$, there exists some $\tau>0$ such that $W''(\phi)\geq \tau$ on $\mathbb R\backslash[-R,R]$ for some $R>0$. We have shown, in particular, that $u_0$ is uniformly bounded in $\overline{\Omega}$. Since $\bar u$ is positive from \eqref{derivative-positive}, then there exists $\kappa\geq 0$ such that $\abs{u_0}<\kappa \bar u$ in $B^+_R$. We set $v:=\kappa \bar u-u_0$, and note that $v$ satisfies the conditions of Proposition \ref{prop-weak-comparison}. Thus we can conclude that $v\geq 0$ in $\overline{\mathbb R^2_+}$ so that $u_0\leq\kappa\bar u$. An analogous argument gives that $-u_0<\kappa\bar u$. We have proved that $\abs{u_0}<\kappa\bar u$ on $\overline{\mathbb R^2_+}$ and, in particular, $\abs{w(x)}<\kappa\phi'(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$.\\ The next step is to decrease $\kappa$ up to the first point where $\kappa\bar u$ touches $\abs{u_0}$: assume, without loss of generality, that for some $\kappa^*\geq 0$ there exists $(x_0,y_0)\in\overline{\mathbb R^2_+}$ such that \begin{equation} \kappa^* \bar u=u_0 \quad \mbox{at }(x_0,y_0)\quad \mbox{and}\quad \kappa^*\bar u \ge u_0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad \overline{\Omega}.\end{equation} We set $d_1:=\max\{W''(\phi),\tau\}$, and $d_2:=d_1-W''(\phi)$. We note that both are non-negative functions on $\mathbb R$ and $d_1(x)\geq \tau$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$. Let $v:=\kappa^*\bar u-u_0\ge 0$, that is a weak supersolution of \begin{equation*}\left\{\begin{split} &\Delta v = 0 \quad &\mbox{ in } \Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial \nu} +d_1 v=d_2 v \geq 0\quad &\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega. \end{split}\right.\end{equation*} We are in the hypothesis of Lemma \ref{lema-comparison}, that can be applied because the functions have enough regularity (in particular $v\in\mathcal C^{1,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\overline\Omega)$). However, because of \eqref{functions-touch} we necessarily must have $v\equiv 0$. We have shown that $u_0\equiv\kappa^*\bar u$, which at the boundary translates as $w\equiv\kappa^*\phi'$.\\
nodes.statement_short: If $\lambda=0$, sliding $\kappa\bar u$ down to touch $u_0$ and strong comparison force $u_0=\kappa^*\bar u$, contradicting $u_0\in H_0$.

nodes.name: Step 6: Conclusion
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 6: Conclusion.} The multiplier $\lambda$ in \eqref{eq::100} must be non-negative.
